title: The Fante States and Their Constitution

pages.text: Walk through Anomabo, Elmina, or Saltpond and you will meet strange and wonderful buildings. They are made of concrete, painted in bright colours, and crowded with statues: lions, ships, whales, clocks, soldiers, and aeroplanes. These are posuban, the shrines of the asafo companies. Beside them, on festival days, fly flags sewn with pictures and proverbs. The asafo were the fighting men of each Fante town. Their shrines and flags tell you something important about the Fante. Here, power did not belong only to chiefs. Ordinary people were organised, and they expected to be heard.

pages.text: Fante tradition says that the people came south from the Techiman area long ago. They were led by three great men: Oburumankoma, Odapagyan, and Oson, whose names mean the whale, the eagle, and the elephant. They settled at Mankessim, which means the great town, a short way inland from the sea. Near the town was a sacred grove where the leaders were buried and where the priests gave advice on important matters. As the population grew, groups moved out and founded new states, among them Abura, Anomabo, Ekumfi, Nkusukum, and Gomoa.

pages.text: The Fante never joined under one king. Each state kept its own chief, but they met in council at Mankessim when danger threatened. The coast gave them another kind of strength. From the late 1400s, European ships came to buy gold, and forts rose at Elmina, Cape Coast, and Anomabo. Fante traders became the go-betweens, carrying goods between the ships and the peoples of the forest. Many grew wealthy. Some sent their children to the schools in the forts. In time, the Fante coast had more people who could read and write than anywhere else in the country.

pages.text: To the north, Asante wanted a direct road to the coast and its trade. The Fante stood in the way, and from 1806 Asante armies invaded several times. The Fante turned to the British for help, and the British used the chance to increase their own power. By the 1860s, the Fante faced two worries: Asante in the north, and European governments that swapped forts and territories among themselves without asking the people who lived there. The chiefs and the educated men decided that the Fante must unite and govern themselves.

pages.text: In 1868, they formed the Fante Confederation. In 1871, at Mankessim, they wrote down a constitution. It set up an assembly in which chiefs and educated men sat together, a king-president, and a court. It planned taxes to pay for roads and for schools, including schools for girls. This was one of the first written constitutions in West Africa, made by Africans for themselves. The British governor did not welcome it. He had several of the leaders arrested. They were soon released, but the Confederation was weakened, and by 1873 it had come to an end.

pages.text: The idea did not die. In 1897, a new generation met at Cape Coast and formed a society to protect the people’s rights to their land. They sent a team to London, argued their case, and won. Later leaders of the independence movement learned from them. When you see the asafo flags flying at the Aboakyer festival in Winneba or the Fetu Afahye in Cape Coast, remember what stands behind the colour and the drumming. The Fante showed that many small states could agree on written rules and govern themselves. Ghana’s own constitution rests on the same belief.

activities.question: According to tradition, where did the Fante first settle near the coast?
How did many Fante traders become wealthy?
options: By mining gold in the forest
By acting as go-betweens for European ships and inland peoples

activities.question: What was special about the 1871 Mankessim constitution?
options: It was a written plan for self-government, made by Africans
It was written by the British governor
It made one chief the ruler of all Ghana

activities.question: Apply it: Several small community groups want to build a borehole together. Which lesson from the Fante Confederation would help them most?
options: Let the richest group decide everything
Agree on written rules, share the cost, and decide together
Wait for someone from outside to do it

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: European ships begin trading on the coast
Asante armies first invade the Fante states
The Fante Confederation writes its constitution
A society is formed at Cape Coast to protect land rights
